subject: Usefulness of mixed IRT vs. CFA/SEM approaches

messages.author: 87096be9e51acd2d
messages.subject: Usefulness of mixed IRT vs. CFA/SEM approaches
parts:
Hi,

this is a bit annoying, but I'm wondering post-analysis whether using mixedmirt() to what I did made any sense or not. I did "exploratory", "confirmatory" and "explanatory" analysis: first exploratory item analysis to check that items work, then confirmatory analysis that the expected factors load and work sensibly and then did mixed IRT with generalized partial credit model. 

I'm pretty happy how it all turned out, but Reviewer 2 (obviously) questioned whether using IRT makes sense past exploratory phase and suggested that CFA/SEM-based approaches allow for more flexibility on model specification, "as you are not examining differential item functioning or item non-invariance".  I've done all kinds of exploratory analysis with the data, which couldn't be done in CFA/SEM framework, but in the end, the final model was rather "simple". So, I started thinking: if I have model with five factors and every polytomous item loading on single factor, does IRT approach give any specific benefit in comparison to CFA/SEM?


Tuomas Aivelo

messages.author: 62219a92fbcbdd15
messages.subject: Re: Usefulness of mixed IRT vs. CFA/SEM approaches
parts:
Mostly no. There are certain instances in which there are no SEM equivalents, but it sounds like your model and the response function is simple, so I don't see why you'd be sacrificing much by using a categorical indicators SEM approach. 

However, there is no PCM in SEM, but you can use factor mixture models to accomplish similar goals in SEM if you discard the GPCM approach. 

I'm answering this in the spirit of stack exchange, where I might be wrong, but I'm trying to take some burden off Phil.

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Usefulness of mixed IRT vs. CFA/SEM approaches
parts:
Thanks, Christopher, your response is appreciated and on point. 

My only comment to Tuomas' original concerns is that the infamous "Reviewer 2" is being a little unforgiving in their stance. If the criticism is that following up exploratory analyses by way of using confirmatory analysis is a type of 'double data dipping' then I agree it's not optimal without using new data and applying cross-validation methods. But, changing from IRT -> SEM mid analysis doesn't somehow magically solve this problem following an EDA. Perhaps what this reviewer was more interested in is the system of variables with which the test is situated, in which case yes SEM currently provides a nicer framework for studying test information in relation to other regressor variables. But, if the analysis is more about learning the properties of the test first to establish some validity of the instrument then I see little reason to change focus. The SEM version of a five-factor confirmatory model is not automatically superior to the IRT version of the same thing since if the response models are comparable in that they really only differ in their estimation criteria, and therefore have different bias-variance trade-offs in the parameter estimates. HTH.

Phil
